( Nebraska Today ) - Czech President Petr Pavel will visit the University of Nebraska–Lincoln on Sept. 24 for a campus conversation highlighting the longstanding cultural and educational ties between Nebraska and the Czech Republic. Pavel will meet with University of Nebraska–Lincoln Interim Chancellor Katherine S. Ankerson and Dr. Jeffrey P. Gold, president of the University of Nebraska system, before participating in a moderated discussion with the campus community at Kimball Recital Hall. The conversation will focus on Nebraska’s Czech heritage, educational and cultural exchange, and the transatlantic relationship between the two countries. “President Pavel’s visit is an opportunity to recognize the longstanding ties between Nebraska and the Czech Republic and the important role the University of Nebraska–Lincoln has played in that relationship,” Ankerson said. “For more than a century, our university has been a place where Czech language, culture and scholarship have connected generations. “We are honored to welcome President Pavel and to continue building our educational and cultural connections.” The event will begin at 11 a.m. Sept. 24 in Kimball Recital Hall, 1113 R St. Tickets are required and seating is limited. Learn more about how to access free tickets . The University of Nebraska established formal Czech language instruction in 1907, following years of efforts by Czech-American students, community members and state lawmakers. Nebraska was among the first universities in the United States to offer Czech language instruction. The roots of the program date to 1904, when Nebraska students established the Czech Komenský Club to promote the study and preservation of Czech language and culture. Czech immigration has played a significant role in Nebraska’s history. Beginning in the 19th century, immigrants from Bohemia and Moravia established communities statewide, contributing to Nebraska’s cultural, agricultural and civic life. The connections created by those communities continue through cultural organizations, academic programs and exchanges between Nebraska and the Czech Republic. Today, the university is one of the few across the nation to offer Czech language instruction and opportunities for students to study and engage with Czech culture. The university offers students more than 25 different study abroad opportunities. The university also maintains Czech Heritage Collections documenting the history and experiences of Czech Americans. Visiting students from the Czech Republic find additional support at Nebraska, including the Paul Robitschek Scholarship , available to international exchange students affiliated with an accredited postsecondary institution in the Czech Republic. The scholarship was created by Robitschek, a Czech immigrant who came to the United States and built a successful career in chemical and plastics manufacturing. Pavel was elected president of the Czech Republic in January 2023 and took office that March. Before becoming president, he served more than three decades in the Czech military, including as chief of the General Staff of the Czech Armed Forces. From 2015 to 2018, he served as chairman of the NATO Military Committee. The event will be livestreamed for those unable to attend in person. More information, including details on parking and clear bag policy, is available online . Pavel’s visit is part of a larger tour of Nebraska. He will also meet with Gov. https://business-review.eu/lifestyle/tra.text: Romania launches BBC World News tourism campaign with Charlie Ottley Romania is promoting its tourism offer through three films made with British producer Charlie Ottley, airing on BBC World News between November 1 and 29, 2026. Organised by the Ministry of Economy, Digitalisation, Entrepreneurship and Tourism (MEDAT), the campaign includes 20 scheduled broadcasts of the 60-second advertisements. Three films showcasing nature and cultural heritage Each advertisement takes a different approach to presenting the country. “Wild Romania” features landscapes, nature and opportunities for ecotourism and adventure. “Sounds Like Romania” introduces the destination through its natural sounds, while “Romania, So Much More Than Dracula!” uses the legend’s international recognition to draw attention to Transylvania’s natural and cultural attractions. Following Ottley’s efforts, the Dracula-themed film received two additional days of broadcasting on October 30 and 31, including Halloween, ahead of the campaign’s official launch. The ministry says the wider campaign aims to encourage international audiences to explore Romania across all four seasons. International promotion and tourism investment Economy, Digitalisation, Entrepreneurship and Tourism Minister Daniel Zamfir said the Danube Delta’s biodiversity, Romania’s cultural heritage and its spa tourism offer could help distinguish the country within the European tourism market. “We need to promote them better on international markets, while also supporting their development through investment,” Zamfir said in the ministry’s statement. The campaign’s broader objective is to encourage tourists to explore the country’s other attractions and return in different seasons. Romania brings 35 co-exhibitors to WTM London The television campaign coincides with Romania’s participation in World Travel Market London on November 3–5, 2026. MEDAT is organising the national stand, which will bring together 35 co-exhibitors.
